rows.question: How did our carriers' on-time performance change in Q3, especially on reefer?
rows.answer: Overall carrier performance slipped in Q3: on-time pickup fell to 93.1% from 95.4% and on-time delivery fell to 91.8% from 94.0% [1][2]. Reefer was the weakest mode, with on-time delivery down to 87.2% from 92.5%, which the scorecard attributes to the September hurricane disruption and longer produce dwell times [3][4]. Reefer carrier fall-off more than doubled to 4.4% of loads from 2.1% [5]. Produce-stop delay is a cost driver too: September produce detention reached $41,800 versus $23,500 in June, under a policy of 2 free hours then $75 per hour capped at $600 per stop [7][8]. Reefer tender acceptance on Southeast lanes fell to 78% in September, and the pricing desk recommends reopening Q4 contract rates with the top 20 produce shippers rather than waiting for the January bid [6][9].

rows.question: Summarize the broker transparency rule and what Ridgeline must change.
rows.answer: The broker transparency rule requires a broker to keep an electronic record of every brokered transaction for at least three years, including the shipper's payment, the carrier payment, and accessorial charges such as detention [1][2]. A requested record must be delivered electronically within 48 hours, carrier waiver clauses are banned, and fines reach $10,000 per violation, with possible loss of operating authority for repeat violations [3][4][5]. The rule takes effect February 1, 2027; the later August 1, 2027 date applies only to brokers with fewer than 10 employees, which Ridgeline (140 staff) does not qualify for [6]. To comply, Ridgeline must remove waiver clauses from carrier agreements, store shipper and carrier payment amounts on the same TMS load record, and build a 48-hour records request process [5]. Its own September data shows the documentation gap: only 62% of produce detention was billed back because BOLs lacked signed in/out times, so enforcing signed BOL times is the priority fix [7][8]. Carriers also rank transparent load history third among factors that would make them accept a broker's load [9].

claims.quote: Under the broker transparency final rule summarized here, a property broker must keep an electronic record of every brokered transaction for at least three years. rows.question: Under the food traceability requirement, what do we as a broker have to keep or provide on produce loads?
rows.answer: Under that brief, a broker that only transports food is not required to keep traceability lot codes, but it must be able to provide shipping documents within 24 hours when a shipper or receiver asks during a recall [1]. The brief puts the record-keeping duty for lot code, quantity, and origin/destination on shippers and receivers, not brokers [2]. It also says temperature logs are not required by the rule, though receivers may make them a contract condition, which matters for our reefer contracts [3]. The library has no FDA text, retention period, or penalty, so we cannot confirm those for produce loads [4].

rows.question: What did the fall carrier survey say about reefer carriers shrinking or leaving the market, and why?
rows.answer: The fall survey (Mid-South Carrier Pulse, Fall 2026) found that 22% of reefer carriers plan to cut fleet size within six months and 9% are considering leaving reefer for dry van, while only 11% plan to add trucks [1][2]. The reasons for shrinking were insurance premiums (64%), equipment financing costs (51%), and unpaid detention time (47%), and forty-one percent of reefer carriers already refuse loads from at least one shipper over chronic detention [3][4]. For Ridgeline, the detention point matters most: carriers ranked detention paid within 30 days and quick pay as the top reasons they would accept a broker's load [5], and our own Q3 data shows 37 carriers removed mostly for lapsed insurance [6]. The survey document itself states it is a fictional demo document, so its figures should not be treated as real market data [8].

rows.question: What's driving reefer spot rates out of the Southeast this quarter, and what does it mean for our produce shippers?
rows.answer: Southeast reefer spot rates averaged $2.87 per mile in Q3 2026, up 14% from Q2, while dry van on the same lanes rose only 4% [1][2]. The memo attributes the rise to a produce push that ran three weeks longer than usual, the Port of Savannah closure that stranded refrigerated trailers, and a shrinking pool of small reefer fleets [3][4][5]. Diesel in the Southeast is up 31 cents since July, which adds roughly five cents per mile in fuel surcharge [6][7]. For produce shippers, spring contract rates now sit well below market and Ridgeline's Southeast reefer tender acceptance fell to 78% in September, so more of their loads fall to spot at higher cost [8]. The pricing desk recommends reopening Q4 rates with the top 20 produce shippers, adding a separate reefer fuel surcharge line, and booking holiday produce 72 hours ahead instead of 48 [9][10]. Detention is compounding the cost: Ridgeline paid $41,800 in produce detention in September and billed back only 62% of it [11][12], and forty-one percent of reefer carriers say they refuse loads from at least one shipper because of chronic detention [13].
